films.title: Doraemon – Il film: Nobita e il nuovo dinosauro

seen_by.review: Formally impressive, operating with some visual ideas that actually aid rather than come across as gimmicky obstacles. Thought I was going to hate it during the first 30 minutes: the coldness from the central relationship really seeped into the idea. I was getting virtually nothing from it. But, there’s a particular scene about an hour in where the meta-statement finally starts to hit. The final act is good stuff. Really liked the black & white bits, great lingering moments of angst.

believe it or not, I was excusing a lot of the film’s shortcomings for the better part of the first 30-40 minutes.

the god-awful dialogue. the god-awful exposition. the terrible acting from the kids.

because I could see what it was trying to do. and what it was trying to do was a twilight zone episode. what it was trying to do was to bring us back to the golden age of amblin. the masterpieces of spielberg and tobe hooper.
there was a semblance of that magic there. and because of that, I was willing to go along and give it the benefit of the doubt.

I also liked that it took its time before the dinosaurs appeared. they took the right amount of time to establish the family and their dynamic but the problem was that it executed all of it so terribly. the conflict between mcgregor and hathaway was not believable, what the kids said was not natural. compare those kids performances to the kids in jurassic park for a second. night and day.

still, I was with it.

the dinosaurs arrive, the flashing lights work (reminiscent of poltergeist), the designs are solid, the cgi is mostly good, and I loved that they had hair and feathers (finally realistic). overall, the world was decently established.

then the rollercoaster starts and somehow everything gets worse.
the acting gets worse. the writing gets worse. the filmmaking gets worse…

there’s this bizarre visual language in the beginning with split diopters being used constantly in very odd places, sometimes cutting directly from a split-diopter shot to another split diopters shot and then back to a completely normal shot for no apparent reason.
there’s a scene where everyone is sitting around in a circle and it just keeps doing this over and over again. it’s unclear what the intention was. it’s not expressive, or properly stylistic. it’s just jarring.

and then you realize there really isn’t a story to root for because the emotional anchor (ewan and anne) is a mess.
the film overstays its welcome by at least an hour.
(this probably should have been the length of a twilight zone episode)

then the film can never decide how grounded it wants to be.
it spends so much time early on trying to create a believable world, and then suddenly starts picking and choosing when realism matters.

a t-rex does not sneak up behind you.
this is a 20,000 pound animal. you’d hear it and the ground would shake. but they don’t hear it for “comedic effect” but even that doesn’t work.

then you have moments like the t-rex going after hathaway and somehow being stopped by a couple of home pillars that an animal of that size would obviously destroy.
and normally i wouldn’t even care about things like that, but when a film establishes a certain level of groundedness and then abandons it whenever it needs a joke or an action beat, you stop knowing what the rules are, and therefore stop suspending your disbelief.

the emotional scenes have the same problem.

mcgregor and hathaway’s relationship is so badly written and so underdeveloped that none of it lands. there’s a moment where they’re trapped together in the car thinking they’re about to die, and for maybe a second you think there could actually be something there.

and then the scene ends before it has time to breathe. before it has time to say anything. before you have time to feel anything.
not that the character development was really there to begin with, but I’m just saying.

and then there’s the dumbass subplots.

my god.

the little boy being chased down and punched because he broke someone’s brother’s arm could have been removed entirely in the edit and absolutely nothing would change. i genuinely can’t believe those scenes survived into the final cut.

the subplot with the girl is slightly less terrible, but still adds almost nothing.
and the longer the film goes, the more convoluted it becomes until eventually it just collapses into absolute nothingness.

the resolution is rushed, anticlimactic and completely underwhelming.

i’m still giving it a couple of stars because of those first 30-40 minutes, where I did feel a little bit of that old amblin magic.

it’s as bad as it follows.

and yes, much worse than the odyssey.

films.title: Il Fuoco Che Ti Porti Dentro

seen_by.review: There is no review for this diary entry. Add a review?
justified alcoholic. can’t believe that ending had my eyes watering.

I often talk in my recent letterboxd reviews about how i struggled to connect with the stories being told or the characters being portrayed in most of the films I’ve recently seen. and sometimes i actually wondered whether I was the problem.
and then a film like this comes along, and i’m reminded that of course not, the film is the problem.

because when a filmmaker truly knows what he’s doing, when he’s a master of his craft like Koreeda is, he grabs you before you have time to blink, immerses you in his world, and doesn’t let go until the credits roll.

this is a return to form for him.
after one of the greatest debuts of all time with maborosi, and the sophomore major masterpiece that is still walking, the level of his work had somewhat declined over the years. but here, he’s back at the top of his game.

this is brilliant.

koreeda has this extraordinary ability to frame humans within nature, to bring the two together in compositions that are so colorful, so cohesive, and so moving.
and it’s not simply a matter of beautiful shots. it’s the choice of lenses, the grain, the colors of the costumes against the locations, the dreamlike editing… the artistry to it all is almost overwhelming.

and of course, this comes directly from the lineage of ozu, whose cinema shares so much of that sensitivity. koreeda is his greatest successor, and god is he worthy of that mantle!

the score is also wonderful, although not quite at the level of sakamoto, whose music brought something so unique to the other works of koreeda.
but beyond the visual artistry, the structure is lovely, and the relationship between the two protagonists is chef’s kiss. the whole thing is such a love letter to animation, to the creative process, but more broadly to friendship and the human endeavor of making art. and intertwined with all of that is this exploration of grief, expressed with subtlety and unbelievable poetry.

does it occasionally go a little overboard? sure. there are moments when i think a little more restraint would have made it even stronger.

I could have spent hours in that world crying, but alas, it had to end…

one of the best films of the year for sure.

PS: I have not seen the anime this is based on, and I’m glad I didn’t.

seen_by.review: There is no review for this diary entry. Add a review?

most people know, that apart from three billboards, I don’t really care for mcdonagh’s films. didn’t care for in bruges, and didn’t care for banshees… they’re fine films but that’s about it.

wild horse nine on the other hand… brilliant. and i’m the first surprised by just how good this is.

it’s profound and heartfelt, and somehow manages to speak about the geopolitical state of our world while remaining incredibly intimate and primarily focused on its characters and their plight.
on top of that, it’s hilarious! those first thirty minutes are among the funniest openings i’ve seen in a long time. as funny as the first thirty minutes of north by northwest!

malkovich is incredibly touching, and his chemistry with rockwell is wonderful. the way their relationship grows, and how the film gradually becomes this meditation on life and regret...
what do we think about when we’re approaching the end of our lives?

the words mcdonagh writes are unbelievably insightful, and malkovich delivers those words with incredible realness, no matter how dark it gets. it’s all completely absurd, and that’s exactly how it’s supposed to be.

a lovely surprise. and genuinely one of the best films of the year.

digger still on top tho.
